gap: No result ChatGPT got works out how hard each adapter is pushed on a current Tesla Wall Connector. Tesla caps that charger at 48 A / 11.5 kW, so every candidate delivers the same 11.5 kW. That puts the Lectron 48A at 100% of its rating for the whole session, the TeslaTap Mini 60A at 80%, and the 80 A Lectron and A2Z at 60%. Per kW delivered, the cost runs from $8.68 (Lectron 48A) to $11.28 (Lectron 80A) to $16.92 (TeslaTap Mini 60A).
standout_why: I compared against evandcharger.com (best NACS-to-J1772 list, 2026-10-05) and thechargecurve.com (Lectron vs A2Z, 2026-10-17). thisWATT, the main cited rival, would not load (certificate error), so I couldn't check it. evandcharger works out kW and $/kW at each adapter's own rating (Lectron $169.99 / 19.2 kW = $8.85/kW). It never uses the charger's 48 A output, and it says nothing about how much of each adapter's rating is in use. The Charge Curve says a home Wall Connector tops out at 48 A and that a 48 A adapter isn't the bottleneck. That covers part of the speed point. Neither page gives the percentage of rating in use at 48 A, the cost per kW actually delivered, or today's $129.99 Lectron 80A price.
decides: This backs the Lectron 80A UL 2252 as the pick. On a 48 A Wall Connector it charges no faster than the 48 A model. Its case is that it runs at 60% of rating where the old 48A runs at 100% with no temperature sensor stated, and today it costs only $30 more ($129.99 vs $99.99). The TeslaTap Mini 60A costs about 50% more per kW delivered than the Lectron 80A ($16.92 vs $11.28). It also states no UL listing, so it stays a niche pick. The Lectron 80A has dropped to $129.99 from the $149.99 on our page and in ChatGPT's answer, and the page price should be updated.
